For every claim you make, state where the information comes from - for example: the specific database, dataset, or tool query you used; the publication (with full citation); or your general training knowledge. If you are uncertain or do not have a source, say so explicitly rather than guessing.

results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. The calyx is closest to the cortex and receives sensory interneuron afferents. The pedunculus is a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes. The mushroom body lobe system consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch, which have different structures at different life stages.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: There are multiple types of Kenyon cells in the adult Drosophila brain, including [KCab-c(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), [KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain"), [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, Kenyon cells can be classified into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which are further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and main. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain").

results.title: Basic connectivity
results.question: What are the main input neurons to the mushroom body?
results.response: The main input neurons to the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the projection neurons from the antennal lobe and sensory interneuron afferents to the calyx.

results.title: Gene expression
results.question: What neurotransmitter do mushroom body Kenyon cells use?
results.response: Mushroom body Kenyon cells, such as alpha/beta core Kenyon cells, use acetylcholine as their primary neurotransmitter. VFB does not currently hold data on other neurotransmitters that alpha/beta core Kenyon cells may use.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. Specifically, antennal lobe projection neurons send synaptic output to the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn. VFB does not currently hold data on other brain regions that the antennal lobe may connect to.

results.title: Cell count
results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?
results.response:
Approximately more than 125,000 neurons.

**Published neuron-count estimates — adult central brain** (from the literature):

- more than 125,000 neurons (adult Drosophila central brain connectome/model) — A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing. — PMID 39358519
- ~139,255 neurons (whole adult Drosophila brain) — Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain. — PMID 39358518

_VFB has annotated 9,413 neuron types with some part in adult central brain — a curated annotation count, not the biological total._

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response: The main components of the central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the paired noduli, the asymmetrical bodies, and the protocerebral bridge. These components are associated with functions such as navigation/orientation, locomotor control, and sleep/arousal or memory-related behaviours.

results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response: Dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons comes from specific types of dopaminergic neurons, including PPL1 and PAM neurons. The dopaminergic PPL1 neuron provides input to the adult [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons comes from dopaminergic PAM neuron 6. The evidence does not specify which DAN types connect to which MBON types, as the term "DAN types" is not matched in the available data.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111763 "Open lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") is located in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind, with distinct dendritic arbors in each lobula plate layer. It detects looming stimuli and its activity elicits a jump escape response. The LPLC2 neuron has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B of the lobula, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4. Its arbors span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells. The LPLC2 neuron projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe and they are cholinergic. VFB does not currently hold data on the specific connections of the LPLC2 neuron beyond its projection to the PVLP.

results.title: Comparative anatomy
results.question: How does the organisation of the antennal lobe compare between adult and larval Drosophila?
results.response: The organisation of the [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") compares between adult and larval Drosophila in terms of glomerular organization, with adults having approximately 50 glomeruli and larvae having around 22 glomeruli.

results.title: Publications for a circuit
results.question: What publications describe the PPL1 dopaminergic neurons and their role in aversive memory?
results.response: Publications describing the dopaminergic PPL1 neurons and their role in aversive memory include Claridge-Chang et al., 2009, Mao and Davis, 2009, Budnik and White, 1988, and Ren et al., 2016. The dopaminergic PPL1 neurons have cell bodies located in the posterior inferior lateral protocerebrum and project to various parts of the mushroom body. These neurons are involved in the formation of labile aversive memory and are part of dopamine-modulated neural circuits regulating aversive taste and odor memories.

results.question: Are there neurons in the Hemibrain dataset that are morphologically similar to the fru+ mAL neurons described in light microscopy studies?
results.response: The Hemibrain dataset contains neurons morphologically similar to the fru+ mAL neurons described in light microscopy studies. Neurons with similar morphology include the [adult fruitless aDT-b neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052693 "Open adult fruitless aDT-b neuron in Virtual Fly Brain").

results.title: Bidirectional connectivity
results.question: Are there reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs)? Which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity?
results.response: There are reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons. VFB found 5 reciprocal class-level pairs between these two neuron types. The top partners for mushroom body output neurons and dopaminergic neurons have been identified, with 84 and 98 partner counts, respectively. VFB does not currently hold data on the specific pairs with the strongest mutual connectivity beyond these counts.

results.title: Pathway tracing
results.question: Trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. What are the intermediate neuron types and their connections?
results.response: A pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the [adult lateral horn](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007053 "Open adult lateral horn in Virtual Fly Brain") involves intermediate neuron types. Antennal lobe projection neurons receive olfactory input in the antennal lobe and send axons to higher brain centers. VFB does not currently hold data on the specific connections of these intermediate neurons to the adult lateral horn.

results.response: More than 1000 matches are found for subclasses of visual system neuron, indicating a complex classification of neuron types. These are organised hierarchically. results.title: Shared connectivity
results.question: Do the alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on any of the same downstream MBON types? Which MBONs receive input from both?
results.response: The [alpha/beta Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100248 "Open alpha/beta Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") converge on some of the same downstream [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types. VFB does not currently hold data on which specific mushroom body output neurons receive input from both alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response: The anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure is: DA1 glomerulus -> adult olfactory antennal lobe glomerulus -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain.

results.title: Cross-region connectivity
results.question: What neuron types connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, and how strong are these connections?
results.response: The [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain") through several neuron types, including [PFL1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111433 "Open PFL1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL2_PB4](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111453 "Open PFL2_PB4 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL3_PB7](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111450 "Open PFL3_PB7 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL1_PB1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111434 "Open PFL1_PB1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [PFL1_PB7](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111440 "Open PFL1_PB7 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [PFL1_PB2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111435 "Open PFL1_PB2 in Virtual Fly Brain"). VFB does not currently hold data on the strength of these connections.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior. It has a large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum and a large descending axon that enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle and descends on the ipsilateral side in the dorsal cervical fasciculus. The giant fiber neuron has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons. It also arborizes in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget. 

The giant fiber neuron connects to various neurons, including [adult VNC neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00059289 "Open adult VNC neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [thoracic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00001983 "Open thoracic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [secondary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047096 "Open secondary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch OFF hemilineage neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049540 "Open Notch OFF hemilineage neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [mesothoracic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00001985 "Open mesothoracic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [primary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047097 "Open primary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch OFF hemilineage secondary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049542 "Open Notch OFF hemilineage secondary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [prothoracic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00001984 "Open prothoracic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch ON hemilineage neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049539 "Open Notch ON hemilineage neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [NB2-4 lineage neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048927 "Open NB2-4 lineage neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Notch ON hemilineage secondary neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049541 "Open Notch ON hemilineage secondary neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [input/output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00053396 "Open input/output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain").

VFB does not currently hold data on available driver lines for the giant fiber neuron. Relevant publications for the study of the giant fiber neuron include Thomas and Wyman, 1984; Koto et al., 1981; Namiki et al., 2018; Power, 1948; Ito et al., 2014; Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Matsuo et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2020.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response: Neuron types that might mediate a connection between the visual system and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") include projection neurons and visual projection neurons. Adult visual projection neurons to the mushroom body have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body. This suggests that visual information could reach the memory circuit via these neurons.

results.title: Novel circuit exploration
results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response: The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") suggests that temperature information could influence memory formation. Thermosensory projection neurons relay temperature-detecting neurons to higher brain centers, and connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body has been found, including connections to mushroom-body-associated dopaminergic neurons and gamma main Kenyon cells. This connectivity supports a plausible thermosensory influence on mushroom-body memory circuitry through thermosensory projection neurons. VFB holds records for various neuron types, including input/output neurons, projection neurons, and local neurons, which may be relevant to understanding the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body.

results.title: Data availability survey
results.question: I'm interested in studying the subesophageal zone (SEZ). How well-characterised is this region in VFB? What neuron types are annotated, what connectomics data is available, and what genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons?
results.response:
The [subesophageal zone](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00051068 "Open subesophageal zone in Virtual Fly Brain") is characterised with available imagery and neuron type annotations. Neuron types with some part in the subesophageal zone can be determined by running a query. 

Genetic tools exist for subesophageal zone neurons, including GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers. There are [4205](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in subesophageal zone") genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the subesophageal zone, including expression patterns such as P{GMR12D05-GAL4} and P{VT000003-GAL4}. 

VFB does not currently hold data on the specific connectomics data available for the subesophageal zone.

results.response: The class summarised connectivity from the [medulla](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003748 "Open medulla in Virtual Fly Brain") includes neurons with presynaptic terminals in medulla, neurons with postsynaptic terminals in medulla, and neurons with synaptic terminals in medulla. These neurons have some part in the medulla. Additionally, there are tracts and nerves innervating the medulla. VFB does not currently hold data on a complete graph form of the class summarised connectivity from the medulla.

results.title: Project identity
results.question: What is Virtual Fly Brain and who is it for?
results.response: Virtual Fly Brain is an interactive tool for neurobiologists to explore the detailed neuroanatomy, neuron connectivity, and gene expression of Drosophila melanogaster.

results.title: Citation
results.question: How should I cite Virtual Fly Brain in a publication?
results.response:
To cite Virtual Fly Brain in a publication, use the provided citation formats below.

```
@article{Court_2023,
author = {Robert Court and Marta Costa and Clare Pilgrim and Gillian Millburn and Alex Holmes and Alex McLachlan and Aoife Larkin and Nicolas Matentzoglu and Huseyin Kir and Helen Parkinson and Nicolas H. Brown and Cahir J. O'Kane and J. Douglas Armstrong and Gregory S. X. E. Jefferis and David Osumi-Sutherland},
title = "{Virtual Fly Brain—An interactive atlas of the Drosophila nervous system}",
journal = {Frontiers in Physiology},
volume = {14},
publisher = {Frontiers Media {SA}},
year = {2023},
month = {jan},
abstract = "{As a model organism, Drosophila is uniquely placed to contribute to our understanding of how brains control complex behavior. Not only does it have complex adaptive behaviors, but also a uniquely powerful genetic toolkit, increasingly complete dense connectomic maps of the central nervous system and a rapidly growing set of transcriptomic profiles of cell types. But this also poses a challenge: Given the massive amounts of available data, how are researchers to Find, Access, Integrate and Reuse (FAIR) relevant data in order to develop an integrated anatomical and molecular picture of circuits, inform hypothesis generation, and find reagents for experiments to test these hypotheses? The Virtual Fly Brain (virtualflybrain.org) web application & API provide a solution to this problem, using FAIR principles to integrate 3D images of neurons and brain regions, connectomics, transcriptomics and reagent expression data covering the whole CNS in both larva and adult. Users can search for neurons, neuroanatomy and reagents by name, location, or connectivity, via text search, clicking on 3D images, search-by-image, and queries by type (e.g., dopaminergic neuron) or properties (e.g., synaptic input in the antennal lobe). Returned results include cross-registered 3D images that can be explored in linked 2D and 3D browsers or downloaded under open licenses, and extensive descriptions of cell types and regions curated from the literature. These solutions are potentially extensible to cover similar atlasing and data integration challenges in vertebrates.}",
```

results.title: API: REST endpoints
results.question: How can I query Virtual Fly Brain programmatically using the SOLR or Owlery API?
results.response: To query Virtual Fly Brain programmatically, you can use the SOLR or Owlery API. The Owlery API provides OWL reasoning services, enabling complex queries over class hierarchies and relationships, and can be accessed at https://owl.virtualflybrain.org/. Various operations are available, such as GET /kbs/vfb/subclasses, GET /kbs/vfb/superclasses, GET /kbs/vfb/equivalent, GET /kbs/vfb/satisfiable, and GET /kbs/vfb/instances. The SOLR Search API provides fast text search and autocomplete functionality for Virtual Fly Brain entities, datasets, and publications.

results.title: API: integrations
results.question: How do I explore Virtual Fly Brain neurons using Navis or pymaid?
results.response:
To explore Virtual Fly Brain neurons, you can use the pymaid library to interface with a CATMAID server and retrieve neuron data. You can connect to the VFB CATMAID server using the `connect_catmaid` function and then use the `get_neurons` function to retrieve a neuron based on its ID. The retrieved neuron data can be plotted using the `navis.plot3d` function.

```python
import pymaid
import navis

navis.set_pbars(jupyter=False)
pymaid.set_pbars(jupyter=False)

# Connect to the VFB CATMAID server hosting the FAFB data
rm = pymaid.connect_catmaid(server="https://fafb.catmaid.virtualflybrain.org/", api_token=None, max_threads=10)

# Test call to see if connection works 
print(f'Server is running CATMAID version {rm.catmaid_version}')

# Find a neuron from its ID (16) -> this is an olfactory projection neuron
n = pymaid.get_neurons(16)

# Plot CatmaidNeuron with navis
navis.plot3d(n, width=1000, connectors=True, c='k')
```

VFB's documentation does not appear to cover pymaid.

results.title: Anatomy teaching diagrams
results.question: Is there a circuit diagram of the mushroom body available on Virtual Fly Brain?
results.response: There is a schematic representation of the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") available on Virtual Fly Brain, which shows the compartmental organisation of the [adult mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003684 "Open adult mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") lobes, including how the dendrites of mushroom body output neurons and the axon terminals of dopaminergic neurons tile the lobes into a stereotyped grid of 15 compartments.
